Subject: RFP: topology, segmentation & threat appendix

Hi Hannah,

Thanks for the quick turnaround on the RFP intake. To close our security review we need an annotated network topology (layered zones, egress and control-plane pathways) and a concise threat-summary that maps likely attack vectors to your mitigations. Key asks from our side:

- Single-page annotated diagram for our architecture doc (PDF)
- Summary of isolation model (how customer workloads are scoped)
- Egress controls, outbound proxies, and permitted endpoints list
- Evidence mapping to SOC2 controls (glossary OK)

I've attached our security questionnaire (Orbis_RFP_Sec_QA_v3.xlsx) — a few items are critical path for procurement. Can you also point us to any demo or walkthrough that explains how you handle cross-tenant KV/cache leakage risk?

We'd like the materials by EOD Tuesday (our timezone). Let me know if that timeline works.

Thanks,
Samira Ross
Lead Security Architect
Orbis Financial Services
Security / Third-Party Risk

From: Hannah Schmitt <hannah_schmitt@redwood.com>

Date: Fri, 10 May 2028 13:45:12 -0700

Samira —

Thanks for the clear list. We've prepared an initial packet and attached: redwood_topology_v1.pdf (annotated diagram), threat_model_summary_v1.docx (2-page executive summary + mapped mitigations), and an evidence matrix CSV that maps items from your spreadsheet to our artifacts. Highlights below:

- Delivery: PDF shows 4 logical zones (Control Plane, Inference Pool, Management/Telemetry, Customer-Connector). Each zone has explicit ACLs and tenant tags.
- Isolation model: Tenants are scoped at the request-routing and KV-cache layer with per-tenant namespaces; model weights are shared by default (open-models) but customer data and prompts never persist in shared cache beyond request window unless explicitly enabled.
- Egress: All outbound flows exit via egress proxies with allowlists and per-customer egress policies; external storage endpoints must be registered via allowlist.
- KV/Cache leakage: We use deterministic namespacing + sharded KV caches and a short time-to-live (configurable). Also per-tenant crypto-wrapping for any persisted metadata.

Two clarifying questions: Do you need packet-level flow logs or flow summaries (we provide both; packet dumps are off by default)? And would you like the diagram in PNG for embedding into your doc set?

I'll loop in Karthik for the technical breakdown. We can meet early next week for a walkthrough if helpful.

Best,
Hannah Schmitt
Sr. Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
hannah_schmitt@redwood.com

Attachments: redwood_topology_v1.pdf; threat_model_summary_v1.docx; evidence_matrix.csv

Samira — quick technical addendum to Hannah's packet below (forwarded for visibility). I've annotated the diagram (see page 1 notes) but listing key elements here for your reviewers: 

1) Logical zones and enforcement points
  - Control Plane (authn, model management): runs in a dedicated management VPC; access is via mTLS and short-lived tokens; strict RBAC enforced via KMS-integrated identity service.

2) Inference Pool (customer workloads): GPU-backed instances in isolated compute pools. Tenancy model is "pooled with soft-namespace": compute is shared for efficiency but each request is tagged and logically isolated in the runtime. Isolation controls: per-request tokenization, KV namespace partitioning, GPU memory zeroization on eviction, and continuous audit hooks.

3) Customer Connector (VPC Peering / PrivateLink): For Private deployments we provide a dedicated connector inside customer VPC (no public IP). For Hosted customers, we support TLS tunnels with mutual auth and egress policies applied on the Redwood side.

4) Egress & Observability: All outbound HTTP/HTTPS passes through an egress proxy cluster with allowlist enforcement; DNS is controlled via resolver policies; logs are retained according to customer SLA. Flow logs are published to the secure telemetry VPC and can be exported to customer SIEM via a push gateway.

5) Threat scenarios we prioritized (samples):
   - KV cache cross-tenant access: mitigation = strict namespace + read-guards + TTL + audit alerts.
   - Model prompt exfiltration via crafted outputs: mitigation = ML-output filters, prompt redaction for known secrets, output sampling for drift detection.
   - Lateral movement from compromised operator seat: mitigation = just-in-time bastion with PAM, session recording, operator MFA, and granular operator roles.

6) Evidence & controls: We maintain automated continuous compliance checks (policy-as-code), signed runbooks for incident response, and artifact links to SOC2 test evidence in the attached matrix. For regulated deployments we offer customer-managed KMS (HSM integration + key rotation) and optional air-gapped on-prem packs.

If you want, we can produce a short (20-minute) demo that walks the topology PDF and shows the egress allowlist flow and KV namespace isolation in action. Proposed times: Mon 5/13 09:00-11:00 PT or Tue 5/14 14:00-16:00 PT.

-Karthik
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
